passage: Sudha, you say you want to be just like your team lead, and I understand. I'm Mohit, and at twenty-five I felt the same about my first mentor, a bridge engineer. I copied her handwriting and the way she paused before answering. Then one afternoon I asked why a certain safety margin was set so high, and she said, "Good question. I am not sure anymore. Let me check." She went home, found the standard, and next day admitted she had been wrong about one number. That day I stopped seeing her as a statue and started seeing a person who could be corrected. I loved her more, not less. Keep asking your team lead the hard questions, Sudha. That is how you grow something of your own.

qa.q: What did Mohit copy from the first mentor?
qa.a: Mohit copied her handwriting and the way she paused before answering.

qa.q: Why did Mohit love the mentor more, not less, after the correction?
qa.a: Seeing her check and admit a wrong number made her a real person, whom Mohit could respect without treating her as flawless.

qa.q: What advice does Mohit give Sudha about the team lead?
qa.a: Keep asking hard questions, so that Sudha builds personal judgment instead of only copying.

qa.q: How did the mentor seem to take being questioned?
qa.a: She called it a good question, checked the standard and admitted the error next day, so she welcomed the challenge.

grounding: An elder recalls admiring a mentor, asking hard questions, and learning to see the mentor as a person with flaws.

passage:
Omkar, you talk about your mentor like he's a god. I did that once. Let your Reena aunty tell you how it went.

At twenty-three I joined a newspaper in Pune, and the editor, Mr. Bhonsle, became my hero. His writing was brilliant. I copied his style, his tea, even his way of holding a pen. If he said a story was good, it was good.

Then he killed a story I had worked on for two months, about a factory dumping waste. He said it was "not strong enough". I believed him. Later I found out the factory owner was his friend.

I was so let down I nearly quit journalism.

The turning point was a long talk with an older reporter, Mrs. Shaikh. "He's a fine writer and a flawed man. Take the writing. Keep your own judgment."

After that I still learned from him, but I asked hard questions. And I took the factory story to another paper.

qa.q: What was Reena's killed story about?
qa.a: It was about a factory dumping waste.

qa.q: How did young Reena feel when she found out why the story was killed?
qa.a: She felt deeply let down, disillusioned enough to nearly quit journalism.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Reena's story?
qa.a: Mrs. Shaikh's advice to take the writing but keep her own judgment, after which she asked hard questions and published the story elsewhere.

qa.q: How might Mr. Bhonsle have seen Reena's questions afterwards?
qa.a: He may have been surprised or uncomfortable that she no longer accepted everything he said.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman who admired her mentor blindly, learned he had flaws, and kept learning from him while asking hard questions and trusting her own judgment.

passage:
It was 2 a.m. on the surgical ward, the lights were flickering in the storm, and Baljeet, a second-year resident, watched Dr. Ganga Menon calm a panicking family in thirty seconds flat. He wanted to be exactly like her. He had copied her handwriting on charts, her way of tying a knot, even her habit of tapping the bed rail twice before speaking.

Then she told him to discharge Mr. Pillai in the morning. Baljeet looked at the numbers. The fever hadn't settled. His stomach tightened. She was never wrong, was she?

He almost said nothing. Then he thought: if I only ever agree, I'm not learning anything.

"Ma'am, can I ask something? His fever hasn't come down. Should we wait a day?"

Dr. Menon looked at the chart for a long moment. "You're right. I was going on yesterday's numbers. Good question."

Baljeet felt something new. Not less admiration. A different kind.

qa.q: What was the time on the surgical ward?
What was Baljeet feeling when he noticed the fever hadn't settled?
qa.a: Baljeet felt anxious, his stomach tightening, torn between admiration and doubt.

qa.q: Why was asking the question better than silently agreeing?
qa.a: It used his own judgment for the patient's safety, and showed that learning from a mentor includes asking hard questions.

qa.q: How did Dr. Menon react to Baljeet's question?
qa.a: Dr. Menon considered it seriously, admitted her mistake and praised the question.

grounding: The story shows a young doctor who admires his mentor and copies her, who learns to ask a hard question and see her as a person who can be wrong.
